opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I see it, physical AI — robots, autonomous vehicles, smart spaces — faces a fundamental data problem that language models didn't have in the same way. For LLMs, the internet gave us a huge corpus of text. But for physical AI, the data you really need is interaction data: what happens in the world when an agent takes an action. That kind of data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous to collect in the real world. You can't crash a thousand cars to learn about edge cases, and you can't have robots break things in a factory every day just to gather training examples.

So the idea behind a world foundation model is to build a model that understands how the physical world evolves — essentially a learned simulator. You give it the current state of the world, maybe some video frames, and an action or a prompt, and it predicts what happens next. If you have a good one, it becomes a kind of digital twin of reality that you can use in many ways: to generate synthetic training data, to evaluate a policy before deploying it, to do planning by imagining futures, or to post-train it into a policy model itself.

And the reason we call it a "foundation" model is that building such a thing from scratch is extremely costly. You need massive video data curation, huge compute, and a lot of engineering expertise. Most robotics companies or research labs can't afford to do that individually. So with Cosmos, our goal at NVIDIA is to pre-train these general-purpose world models on large amounts of physically relevant video, and then release them openly, so developers can fine-tune them for their specific setup — their robot, their camera configuration, their environment — with a much smaller amount of data.

In a sense, it's about lowering the barrier. We believe physical AI is going to be the next big wave, and the world model is a key piece of infrastructure for it. Just like GPT-style models became the starting point for language applications, we hope Cosmos can be a starting point for people building physical AI systems.

r001.rationale: The response says building a world model from scratch requires costly data curation, compute, and expertise that most robotics companies or research labs lack, then explains Cosmos is intended to provide general-purpose pretrained models developers can fine-tune.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it starts with a simple observation: the reason large language models worked so well is that the internet gave us an enormous amount of text, and from that text, models learned a kind of model of the world as humans describe it. But physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to act in the real world, cannot learn from text alone. A robot does not need to know how to write a poem about picking up a cup. It needs to know what happens when its gripper closes on the cup, how the cup moves, what happens if it slips. That knowledge is about physics, about space, about time, about cause and effect, and it is not written down anywhere in a form you can simply read.

So where do you get that knowledge? You get it from observing the physical world, which means video. Video is the data modality that actually captures how the world evolves. If you can train a model that watches a huge amount of video and learns to predict what comes next, that model has to internalize something about gravity, object permanence, how light behaves, how materials deform. That is what we mean by a world model: a model that, given the current state of the world and some action, predicts the future state.

The second reason, and in some ways the more practical one, is data scarcity for robotics. With language, the data already existed. For physical AI, every robot is different, every environment is different, and collecting real-world data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. You cannot crash a car ten thousand times to learn how not to crash. A world foundation model lets you generate those experiences, run simulations that are photorealistic and physically plausible, and train the policy on them. It also lets the robot plan, imagine the consequences of an action before taking it.

And the reason we call it a foundation model, and why we open it up, is that training this from scratch is extremely costly. Very few organizations can curate tens of millions of hours of video and spend the compute to train on it. We felt that if we build the general model once and release it, then developers can post-train it for their specific robot, their specific warehouse, their specific driving scenario, the same way people fine-tune a language model today. That is really the bet with Cosmos: that physical AI needs its own foundation layer, and that it should be built on video, because video is where the physics lives.

r001.rationale: The response says physical AI needs a world foundation model, explains that training one from scratch requires costly video curation and compute that very few organizations can afford, and presents Cosmos as a general model developers can post-train for their needs.

astra-6.text:
When we talk about physical AI, we mean AI that can act in the physical world—robots, for example, or autonomous vehicles. To act effectively, these systems need to understand how the world changes and what might happen when they take an action.

The challenge is that learning everything through real-world interaction is expensive and slow. You cannot put a robot into every possible situation, and some situations are dangerous to explore. So we need a way to learn from broader experience and simulate possible outcomes.

That’s the motivation for Cosmos as a world foundation model: to model how the physical world evolves. Given an observation, and potentially an action, it can generate possible future scenarios. That can help us create training data and develop and evaluate systems before putting them into the real world.

The foundation-model part is important because we want a shared starting point that can be adapted to different physical AI tasks, rather than building a separate world model from scratch for every robot or application.

r001.rationale: The response explains Cosmos as a shared world model that avoids building a separate model from scratch for each task, but does not say it was built to meet physical AI companies’ needs or that those companies lack the resources to build such models themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
When we talk about physical AI, we mean AI systems that interact with the physical world, like robots and autonomous vehicles. Those systems need to understand how the world changes over time and what might happen when they take an action. Recognizing what’s in an image is only part of that challenge.

The other challenge is data. Collecting real-world experience is expensive, and it’s difficult to capture every situation a robot or a car might encounter, especially rare or dangerous ones. We need a way to generate diverse experiences without having to stage every scenario in the real world.

That’s the motivation for Cosmos: a world foundation model that learns how the physical world behaves and can generate possible future scenarios. It can help developers create synthetic data and explore situations for training and evaluating physical AI systems. The goal is to make that development process more scalable, while still grounding it in real-world testing.

r001.rationale: The response explains Cosmos’s role in generating synthetic data and scaling physical AI development, but it does not say it meets companies’ need for a world model they lack resources to build from scratch.
